People ask why we get the law wrong, and the honest answer is that we film the true version once, in the first season of everything, and then we never do it again. A truthful hearing is paperwork and waiting. It is four people reading, one of them coughing, and a decision that was taken in an email three weeks earlier. Nothing that matters happens where a camera can see it, and if you shoot it accurately the audience leaves. Now here is the part that surprised me. Lawyers write to us constantly, and almost never about the procedure. They do not care that the objection was impossible. What they write about is the relationship between a junior and a senior. They write when we make a partner cruel in a way that is convenient for the plot, or when we let a trainee win an argument that no trainee would ever be allowed to have. That is the mail I read twice. So the rule in our writers' room is short. We are allowed to be wrong about what a court does, and never about what the job feels like. The first is a convention that everybody in the audience has already agreed to. The second is the only thing the show is actually about.

For about four years I corrected everything out loud, and my wife stopped watching them with me, which was fair. Then I stopped. The errors are a convention, like the fact that nobody in a film ever says goodbye before hanging up the telephone. Everybody knows, nobody minds, and it saves ninety seconds an episode. What I did not expect is how much they get right about the parts my training never covered at all. How much of this work is standing in a corridor with somebody who is frightened and explaining the same thing three times. How rarely the conversation that decides a case happens anywhere near a judge. How often the important thing is said by somebody junior, quietly, and ignored. I did not learn any of that at university. I learned it in the second year of practice, badly. And I will say one more thing, about the students who arrive having watched a great deal of this. They come in wanting a job that does not exist, and a surprising number of them stay for the right reasons once they find out. Given the choice, I would rather teach somebody who came in through a story than somebody who came in through a salary.
